title: National segmentation
text: The page documents the technical decisions made during the segmentation process.

title: National segmentation
text:
Rationale and objective
The South African Biodiversity Intactness Index (BII) requires a consistent spatial unit of assessment to which a broad land-use class, land-use intensity, and eventually species information can be linked. Here, that unit is an image-derived segment: a group of neighbouring 10 m pixels with similar landscape characteristics.
A regular grid (also called a fishnet), that is typically used in broad scale spatial workflows, is straightforward to reproduce, but its boundaries are imposed without reference to the landscape. A grid cell can therefore split fields or plantations, or combine very different land uses, imposing artificial boundaries on the landscape. Segmentation can follow landscape variation more closely, potentially producing units that more closely align with underlying vegetation structure, land use patterns, and management units, which provides a more appropriate basis for assigning land use intensity and estimating biodiversity intactness.
Our aim in this part of the workflow is to select one nationally applicable segmentation configuration that balances land-cover homogeneity, recognisable landscape structure, consistency with the approximately 1 km analysis scale used in the regional BII, and a manageable number of units for national modelling. We tested various options for segmentation below.

title: National segmentation
text:
Input data
Satellite representation. Segmentation uses the 2022 annual Google Satellite Embedding V1 image collection (AlphaEarth Foundations; Brown et al. (n.d.)). This dataset provides a 64-dimensional vector, or landscape fingerprint, for each 10 m pixel, combining patterns learned from multiple Earth-observation sources. The dimensions are not separate land-cover categories or individually interpreted physical measurements. SNIC used all 64 bands simultaneously to group pixels with similar signatures.
The exact Google Earth Engine (GEE) input is:
var embeddings = ee.ImageCollection(
  'GOOGLE/SATELLITE_EMBEDDING/V1/ANNUAL'
).filterDate('2022-01-01', '2023-01-01');
For each test region, the collection is filtered to the region (drawn in GEE), mosaicked and clipped to a 5 km buffer. The comparison runs SNIC on this embedding mosaic, not on the classified SANLC raster: the latter is retained as independent composition data for evaluating the resulting segments. No separate land/water mask is applied in the test-segmentation export script. Terrestrial masks is applied when calculating land-cover proportions in the next processing stage.
Composition data for subsequent evaluation. We will intersect each segment with (1) the broad BII land-use classification derived from 2022 SANLC, and (2) the original detailed SANLC subclasses. The intended GEE sources are:
projects/thicket-ecological-condition/assets/BII_SA/NLC_reclass_BII_land_use_intensity
projects/thicket-ecological-condition/assets/SA_NLC_2022_GEO
The reclassified layer provides the broad BII classes; the detailed SANLC layer allows homogeneity to be assessed within those classes. Protected-area cover will be assessed separately, because it is a management overlay that may overlap other land covers. The exact bands, masks and crosswalk versions are recorded in the separate pages under Land Use Intensity and Segment Allocation.

title: National segmentation
text:
Projection and analysis grid
The processing grid is held fixed for all scenarios. A projected coordinate reference system converts locations on the curved Earth into planar coordinates that can be expressed in metres. Without a fixed projection and pixel grid, the size of an SNIC seed measured in pixels could correspond to different ground distances, and the calculated segmentation could change with the resolution requested by GEE’s map display.
We use SANBI’s South African Albers Equal Area projection, AEA_RSA_WGS84, with the following parameters:



Property
Value




Projection
Albers Equal Area (custom WGS84)


Datum / ellipsoid
WGS84


Central meridian
25° E


Latitude of origin
0°


Standard parallel 1
24° S (-24)


Standard parallel 2
33° S (-33)


False easting and false northing
0 m, 0 m


Map units
metres


Pixel size
10 × 10 m


Affine transform
[10, 0, 0, 0, -10, 0]



The two standard parallels are latitudes where this projection’s area-preserving transformation is anchored. The equal-area property is useful for calculating and comparing land-use areas and proportions throughout South Africa. The specific affine transform additionally fixes the origin and orientation of the 10 m pixel grid, so tests do not shift relative to one another.
The GEE code uses a custom WKT CRS definition, not a generic Web Mercator or geographic latitude/longitude CRS. The exact WKT used in the test is preserved in the reproducible code below. The grid is explicitly assigned to the embedding mosaic using setDefaultProjection(proj); the SNIC result is then forced onto the same grid using .reproject({crs: proj}). Lastly, every export specifies the same crs and crsTransform.
This matters because GEE documents that SNIC can produce different results at different interactive map zoom levels. Forcing a 10 m processing projection prevents the viewer’s zoom level from determining the algorithm’s working resolution. As reproject() can be computationally expensive, it is applied only to the bounded test areas; results were exported as assets before downstream processing. The final selected segment size was then run nationally and used as the fixed segmentation layer for later stages.

title: National segmentation
text:
Algorithm and parameters
We use Simple Non-Iterative Clustering (SNIC), an object-based segmentation algorithm that starts from seed locations and grows connected clusters of spectrally/embedding-similar pixels. SNIC returns a raster in which pixels belonging to a cluster share an integer ID.








Parameter
Current value
Reasoning




Input
2022 annual Satellite Embeddings, all 64 bands
Captures multiple landscape characteristics in a consistent national dataset rather than relying on one spectral band.


Processing CRS
AEA_RSA_WGS84
Metre-based, equal-area reference appropriate for South African area calculations.


Processing pixel size
10 m
Matches the nominal resolution of the embedding data and fixes the interpretation of pixel-based settings.


size
60, 80, 100, 120 pixels
Four seed spacings centred around the approximately 1 km landscape scale of the regional BII. This is the only intentionally varied SNIC parameter.


compactness
1
Balances similarity of the embedding signatures and spatial compactness of the segments.


connectivity
8
Allows side-adjacent and diagonally adjacent pixels to be grouped.


neighborhoodSize
size * 4
Provides a processing neighbourhood larger than the seed spacing to reduce tile-edge artefacts; scaled consistently in all test scenarios.


seeds
Not supplied
SNIC generates its default regularly spaced seed grid; no random seed locations are specified.


Region buffer
5,000 m
Reduces the risk that artificial clipping boundaries influence segments within the test rectangle.


Export ID band
clusters → unit_id
Stores the calculated cluster identifier as an integer raster.


Asset pyramiding
mode
Preserves categorical IDs when assets are viewed at coarser display resolutions.



Important: size specifies initial seed spacing in pixels, not the final segment diameter or area. Actual segment sizes and shapes depend on the embedding patterns and growth of clusters. The nominal meter values are useful scenario labels, but actual segment areas will be measured and reported.

Preliminary exploration showed that connectivity of 8 and compactness settlings of 1 followed natural shapes in the landscape. We thus generated 4 segment “scenarios” with the same parameters settings, only varying size. This isolates the effect of the size parameter more cleanly and makes the eventual national product reproducible.

600 m tests whether finer units capture settlement edges, agricultural fields and small, contrasting land-cover patches sufficiently better to justify the extra segment count.
800 m was included as a candidate segment scale to assess whether it provides an appropriate balance between spatial detail and landscape-scale representation.
1,000 m approximates the linear scale of the original regional BII’s 1 × 1 km mapping grid, while allowing SNIC boundaries to follow spatial patterns rather than fixed squares.
1,200 m tests whether a somewhat coarser representation reduces processing demands without merging ecologically different land uses excessively.

A 1,000 m SNIC seed spacing is not the same as a fixed 1 × 1 km grid. A grid can be retained as an additional reference comparison, but it is not one of the four SNIC sensitivity scenarios.
Earlier exploratory segmentation at other scales suggested that small segments could follow very fine land-cover variation while losing the broader landscape context. Those trials motivated the provisional 800 m layer but were not a controlled four-size comparison. The sensitivity test documented here is intended to provide the quantitative justification for a final choice, rather than assume the earlier choice was optimal.

title: National segmentation
text:
Selection of two test landscapes
We use two heterogeneous mixed-use landscapes, rather than comparing segment sizes only in predominantly natural terrain. Both were chosen because they contain land uses that are easy to combine unintentionally within a large assessment unit, but their spatial configurations differ substantially.








Test site
GEE geometry name
Landscape composition and motivation




Cape Town / surrounding landscape
CT
A well-known mosaic of urban and industrial areas, timber plantations, mountainous natural vegetation, and smallholdings. It tests segmentation at sharp land-use boundaries, along natural–built-up interfaces, and in terrain with strong topographic variation.


Eastern Cape mixed landscape
EC
A fine-grained mosaic of villages, croplands and natural vegetation. It tests whether small, interspersed land uses are separated adequately without creating an excessive number of small fragments.



Testing these contrasting landscapes makes the sensitivity analysis more informative than using only one urban or rural landscape. The samples are purposeful test sites, not statistically representative samples of South Africa; conclusions should be framed as evidence of the method’s behaviour in two challenging land-use mosaics.
The rectangles are drawn in the GEE Code Editor and named CT and EC. Each rectangle is buffered by 5 km for segmentation; the central, unbuffered rectangle is the evaluation area. In particular, segments intersecting the central rectangle boundary will be flagged and can be excluded from summaries that require complete segments. The wider buffered assets can still be displayed for a map figure.

title: National segmentation
National segmentation
text:
Sensitivity analysis and validation plan
The goal of this evaluation is not to validate the broad land use group calculation. It tests whether the spatial units retain meaningful land-use composition, which is the intended input to the BII.
For each of the eight segment assets, we calculated the area and proportion of every mapped broad BII land-use class and, separately, every detailed SANLC subclass within each segment. Pixel areas were summed using ee.Image.pixelArea() and divided by the mapped terrestrial area of the segment. The protected-area proportion was extracted as a separate overlapping attribute, not added to land-cover proportions.
A segment-level CSV export contained:







Field
Meaning




site, scenario, unit_id
Test landscape, nominal seed spacing and segment identifier; IDs are only compared within a given site/scenario.


area_ha
Terrestrial mapped area in hectares.


p_settlement, p_timber, p_treecrop, p_cropland, p_untrans
Proportion of terrestrial area occupied by each mapped broad BII land-use class.


p_protected
Protected-area overlap (not part of the land-cover proportions sum).


assigned_class
Broad class under the agreed >20% sequential allocation rule.


boundary
Flag identifying segments that intersect the core test-rectangle boundary.



A second long-format subclass CSV (site, scenario, unit_id, sanlc_class, area_ha, proportion) retained the full SANLC composition for detailed checks in R. Raster-to-vector conversion of the buffered test IDs (for example to GeoJSON) will supply segment outlines for GIS map figures. The CSV is the analysis output; vectorisation is primarily for cartographic comparison.
We will calculate and compare:

Broad-class homogeneity: the largest land-use proportion in each segment (a value of 1 indicates only one broad class).
Detailed-class homogeneity: the largest original SANLC subclass proportion, distinguishing variation hidden within a broad class.
Mixed-segment frequency: the proportion of segments containing substantial amounts of more than one broad class.
Allocation: for each broad class, the proportion of its mapped area that occurs in segments ultimately assigned to the same class under the 20% decision tree.
Segment-area distribution and counts: the real distribution of segment size and the computational consequences of a finer or coarser assessment unit.

Summaries were calculated both by segment and area-weighted, separately for CT and EC and where relevant by land-use class. These complementary summaries are important: a large number of small fragments should not overwhelm the total mapped landscape, while a few very large natural segments should not conceal poor representation of settlements or croplands.
Planned figures include (a) four identical-scale maps of segment boundaries over the same basemap per study area, (b) homogeneity distributions by scenario, and (c) differences in composition/allocation fidelity by land use. The regular 1 × 1 km grid may be retained as a contextual reference from earlier analyses, but it will not be conflated with the 1,000 m SNIC scenario.

Criteria for deciding the national size
The preferred scenario should show a reasonable balance between higher within-segment homogeneity, preserving small transformed land-use mosaics, recognisable landscape boundaries and national processing feasibility. If the 600 m results provide only limited improvement over 800 m while substantially increasing segment counts, 800 m would remain a reasonable compromise. If results contradict that expectation, the final choice should reflect the evidence. We will report the observed trade-offs and record the final selected size after analysis, rather than present a preferred size as an already validated result.


Results
Land-cover homogeneity declined progressively with increasing SNIC seed spacing across both study areas (Table ?@tbl-segmentation-comparison). The 600 m scenario produced the highest homogeneity but substantially more assessment units, while the 1,200 m scenario showed greater mixing of land-cover classes and reduced retention of transformed land uses. The 800 m and 1,000 m scenarios were therefore considered the most suitable compromises between spatial detail and computational efficiency.
Increasing seed spacing from 800 to 1,000 m reduced the number of segments by 36.9% in CT and 37.6% in EC, with only modest reductions in mean land-cover homogeneity (1.1 and 1.9%, respectively). The proportion of terrestrial area within segments containing at least 80% of a single land-cover class declined by approximately 3 percentage points in both areas. Class-specific allocation also remained broadly comparable, with some reduction in the retention of transformed land uses at larger segment sizes. A 1,000 m seed spacing was therefore selected, providing substantially fewer assessment units with relatively little loss of land-cover homogeneity. The resulting median segment areas (90.2 ha in CT and 88.8 ha in EC) were also broadly comparable to the 100 ha grid cells used in the original sub-Saharan African BII assessment, while retaining the advantage of image-derived segment boundaries. The 1000m segment size is the most practical compromise between land-cover homogeneity, ecological representation and computation efficiency among the tested scenarios.

Table 2. Comparison of segmentation characteristics across four SNIC seed spacings in Cape Town (CT) and the Eastern Cape (EC). Mean homogeneity represents the area-weighted mean proportion of each segment occupied by its dominant broad BII land-cover class. The final column gives the percentage of assessed terrestrial area occurring in segments with at least 80% homogeneous land cover. title: National segmentation
text:
National production and version control
The national layer was generated with the selected size, fixed 10 m Albers settings. The test-area IDs are not presumed to match the eventual national IDs because processing extent and tiling can affect cluster numbering and potentially boundaries.
Before transferring a national segmentation layer to the collaborator who links species information to the segments, we will “froze” the final raster, checked its coverage and unique IDs, preserved its original 10 m grid and CRS, and recorded the exact asset path and generation code. Land-use assignment and intensity can subsequently be updated as attributes without altering the frozen segment geometry or IDs.

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text: This page documents the progress toward creating a national Biodiversity Intactness Index for South Africa. It highlights current status in the land use intensity analysis workflow, describes potential next steps and decisions that still require discussion. At the top of each page we show what still needs to be done.

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text: This page documents the progress toward creating a national Biodiversity Intactness Index for South Africa. It highlights current status in the land use intensity analysis workflow, describes potential next steps and decisions that still require discussion. At the top of each page we show what still needs to be done.

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text:
Workflow summary
This workflow combines the South African National Land Cover (NLC) 2022, the South African National Protected Area Database (SAPAD) and biome-specific ecocsystem condition data to produce segment-based land use and land use intensity layers to develop a South African Biodiversity Intactness Index.
The unit of assessment is a spatial segment rather than an individual raster pixel. At the end of the workflow, each segment receives:

one dominant BII land use class; and
one land use intensity estimate between 0 and 1.

The pages are split into four sections:

National segmentation
National land use reclassification
National segment land use and intensity allocation
Context-specific land use intensity score refinement of “untransformed”

text:

title: Land use intensity
text: We used the South African National Land Cover (SANLC) dataset to assign both the broad land use to each segment and estimate land use intensity because it provides a nationally consistent and high-resolution representation of land cover that was not available across sub-Saharan Africa for the original BII assessment. SANLC is already used by SANBI in the National Biodiversity Assessment and other national biodiversity monitoring applications, providing consistency with established South African biodiversity products. Its regular update cycle (approximately every four years) also means that the BII land use and intensity layers can be updated using the same underlying national dataset, supporting repeatable monitoring of changes through time.

title: Land use intensity
text: We used the South African National Land Cover (SANLC) dataset to assign both the broad land use to each segment and estimate land use intensity because it provides a nationally consistent and high-resolution representation of land cover that was not available across sub-Saharan Africa for the original BII assessment. SANLC is already used by SANBI in the National Biodiversity Assessment and other national biodiversity monitoring applications, providing consistency with established South African biodiversity products. Its regular update cycle (approximately every four years) also means that the BII land use and intensity layers can be updated using the same underlying national dataset, supporting repeatable monitoring of changes through time.

title: Land use intensity
section: Linking intensity to the expert assessments
text:
Linking intensity to the expert assessments
The BII experts estimated the abundance remaining for each species group under specified landscape scenarios, relative to an intact reference. For settlements, croplands and tree croplands, paired scenarios define the low- and high-intensity endpoints of an intensity gradient. Timber plantations were represented by a single intensive scenario.
For the sub-Saharan African BII, separate spatial proxies were used to estimate intensity within each broad land use. Relevant variables were standardised to 0–1, combined with equal weights, and rescaled within each broad land use class. For example, settlement intensity used settlement extent and population density, while cropland intensity used crop cover, field size and nitrogen inputs.
The South African implementation differs slightly because the 73-class SANLC product provides substantially more detailed information on the composition of each landscape. We use those subclasses to represent the within-class intensity of the land use assigned to a segment, while also explicitly accounting for the proportion of the segment converted to any non-natural land use.




SANLC intensity crosswalk
For transparency, the SANLC subclasses used to characterise within-class land use intensity were assigned to low, medium and high intensity categories and converted to scores of 0, 0.5 and 1, respectively. Timber plantations were treated as a single high-intensity class with a fixed score of 1.

These scores represent relative intensity within each broad land use class, rather than a common ecological impact scale across all classes. The final segment-level intensity for non-natural classes is therefore obtained by averaging the assigned-class mean intensity with the total proportion of the terrestrial segment occupied by all non-natural land uses.


Segment intensity calculation
For settlements, croplands and tree croplands, SANLC subclasses are assigned provisional intensity scores:



Intensity class
Score




Low
0


Medium
0.5


High
1



For each segment, the first component is the area-weighted mean intensity of SANLC pixels belonging to the broad land use assigned to that segment:
\[
\bar{I}_{c,s}
=
\frac{\sum_i a_i I_i}
     {\sum_i a_i}
\]
where:

\(\bar{I}_{c,s}\) is the mean subclass intensity for assigned class \(c\) in segment \(s\);
\(I_i\) is the intensity score of pixel \(i\);
\(a_i\) is its area; and
only valid pixels belonging to the assigned broad land use are included.

The second component is the proportion of the terrestrial segment covered by all non-natural BII land uses combined:
\[
P_{\mathrm{non-natural},s}
=
P_{\mathrm{settlement},s}
+
P_{\mathrm{timber},s}
+
P_{\mathrm{treecrop},s}
+
P_{\mathrm{cropland},s}
\]
The final segment intensity for settlements, tree croplands and croplands is:
\[
I_s =
\frac{
\bar{I}_{c,s}
+
P_{\mathrm{non-natural},s}
}{2}
\]
This gives equal weight to:

how intensive the assigned land use is, based on its detailed SANLC subclasses; and
how much of the surrounding segment has been converted away from intact land.

For example, if a settlement-assigned segment has a mean settlement intensity of 0.8 and 90% of its terrestrial area is covered by settlements, croplands, tree croplands or timber plantations, its final intensity is:
\[
I_s = \frac{0.8 + 0.9}{2} = 0.85
\]
This allows two segments assigned to the same broad land use to differ not only because their mapped subclasses differ, but also because one occurs in a more extensively transformed landscape.


Timber plantations
Timber plantations are treated separately because the BII expert elicitation used a single plantation scenario rather than a low-to-high plantation gradient. Their assigned-class intensity is therefore fixed at 1.
The segment-level intensity is still adjusted for the total amount of non-natural land:
\[
I_s =
\frac{
1
+
P_{\mathrm{non-natural},s}
}{2}
\]
Thus, a timber-assigned segment that is 80% non-natural receives an intensity of 0.9.


Protected lands
Protected lands are currently assigned an intensity of 0. Protected status is treated as a management designation rather than part of the non-natural proportion.
This value represents the low-pressure protected scenario used in the BII land use framework and should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of protected-area effectiveness or ecological condition.


Untransformed lands
In progress
Intensity for segments assigned to Untransformed lands will be calculated separately. The land use intensity of land that has not been converted cannot be inferred reliably from SANLC natural cover subclasses alone because natural vegetation may still experience substantial grazing, browsing, harvesting or other land use pressures.
The sub-Saharan BII estimated intensity in untransformed lands primarily from livestock density and nitrogen inputs, with livestock pressure standardised within rainfall and soil nutrient contexts. For the South African implementation, additional pressure and condition datasets can be used where they improve on these broad proxies.
Potential inputs include livestock pressure relative to carrying capacity and mapped degradation or condition products being developed at SANBI. For example, in the Thicket biome, remotely sensed estimates of intact, moderately degraded and severely degraded vegetation could help distinguish rangeland use intensity within segments otherwise classified as untransformed.
This component will be developed separately so that transformation intensity in the four non-natural classes is not conflated with ecological pressure or degradation in remaining natural vegetation.

title: Land use intensity
text:
Class-specific implementation

Settlements
Endpoints: mixed settlements → dense urban.

The South African approach uses SANLC settlement subclasses to distinguish within-class intensity. Vegetated formal and informal residential areas and villages are assigned intermediate scores, highly transformed residential, commercial, industrial, transport and mining classes are assigned high scores, and urban recreational classes are assigned low scores.
The mean settlement score is then averaged with the total non-natural proportion of the segment.


Croplands
Endpoints: non-intensive smallholder croplands → intensive large-scale croplands.


Commercial annual crops, sugarcane and other intensive commercial crop classes are assigned high intensity. Subsistence/small-scale annual crops and SANLC smallholding classes are assigned to the Croplands broad class at low intensity, reflecting the non-intensive smallholder endpoint more closely.
The mean cropland score is then averaged with the total non-natural proportion of the segment.


Tree croplands
Endpoints: non-intensive smallholder croplands → tree-crop plantations.

Commercial orchards and vines are currently assigned high intensity. Their mean assigned-class intensity is averaged with the total non-natural proportion of the segment.


Timber plantations
Single scenario: timber plantations.

All plantation subclasses are treated as the single intensive plantation scenario. Their assigned-class intensity is fixed at 1 and averaged with the total non-natural proportion.

title: Land use intensity
section: Difference from the sub-Saharan BII approach
text:
Difference from the sub-Saharan BII approach
The two approaches share the same conceptual aim: representing the intensity of human land use at a landscape scale so that mapped land uses correspond as closely as possible to the scenarios assessed by experts.
The main difference is how intensity is “spatialised”.
The sub-Saharan BII relied on separate pressure proxies such as population density, mapped land use extent, field size, nitrogen inputs and livestock density. These variables were standardised and combined to produce a relative intensity score within each broad class.
The South African BII makes greater use of the detailed SANLC classification. The intensity of the assigned class is first estimated from its mapped subclasses and then combined with the total proportion of the segment occupied by non-natural land uses. This explicitly incorporates landscape transformation into the segment score and reduces the dependence on separate continental-scale intensity proxies where detailed national land-cover information is available.
The approach remains consistent with the landscape-scale interpretation of the expert elicitation: intensity is intended to characterise the overall human modification represented by a segment, rather than the condition of an isolated land-cover pixel.

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
text:
We used the South African National Land Cover (SANLC) dataset to assign broad land use and estimate land use intensity because it provides a nationally consistent and high-resolution representation of land cover that was not available across sub-Saharan Africa for the original BII assessment. SANLC is already used by SANBI in the National Biodiversity Assessment and other national biodiversity monitoring applications, providing consistency with established South African biodiversity products. Its regular update cycle (approximately every four years) also means that the BII land use and intensity layers can be updated using the same underlying national dataset, supporting repeatable monitoring of changes through time.
The aim of this section of the workflow is to assign each segment one dominant BII land use class following an expert decision tree.

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
Segment land use and intensity allocation
section: 2. Assign one BII land use class
text:
2. Assign one BII land use class
A candidate class becomes eligible for assignment when it covers more than 20% of the segment.
The classes are evaluated in the following priority order:

Settlements
Timber plantations
Tree croplands
Croplands
Protected lands
Untransformed lands

Where multiple classes exceed 20%, the class with the highest priority is assigned. Therefore the decision tree logic is:
IF settlement proportion > 0.20 assign Settlement
ELSE IF timber proportion > 0.20 assign Timber plantation
ELSE IF tree-crop proportion > 0.20 assign Tree cropland
ELSE IF cropland proportion > 0.20 assign Cropland
ELSE IF protected proportion > 0.20 assign Protected land
ELSE assign Untransformed land
Example, if:

settlement proportion = 0.25;
cropland proportion = 0.30; and
both exceed 0.20.

The segment is assigned to Settlements, because settlements have higher priority than croplands.

Examples








Segment composition
Assigned class
Reason

Croplands
Settlement does not exceed 20%, but cropland does

Timber plantations
Both exceed 20%, but timber has higher priority

Protected lands
Protected cover exceeds 20% and no higher-priority class does

Untransformed lands
No other class exceeds 20%

Settlements
Transformed land is assigned before protected land



Note, a higher-priority transformed land use can override the protected assignment.
The allocation logic is implemented in reverse order in GEE because later where() statements overwrite earlier assignments. In other words, “where” the condition is true, replace the current value with the specified class.
var assignedLandUse = ee.Image(BII_UNTRANSFORMED)

  .where(
    propProtected.gt(0.20),
    BII_PROTECTED
  )

  .where(
    propCropland.gt(0.20),
    BII_CROPLAND
  )

  .where(
    propTreeCrop.gt(0.20),
    BII_TREE_CROP
  )

  .where(
    propTimber.gt(0.20),
    BII_TIMBER
  )

  .where(
    propSettlement.gt(0.20),
    BII_SETTLEMENT
  )

  .rename('bii_land_use');

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
Segment land use and intensity allocation
text:
Output
The final spatial product is a two-band raster:
bii_land_use
bii_land_use_intensity

Band 1: bii_land_use
An integer value from 1 to 6 representing the dominant BII land use class assigned to each segment.


Band 2: bii_land_use_intensity
A continuous value from 0 to 1 representing segment-level land use intensity. For non-natural classes, this combines the within-class intensity of the assigned land use with the proportion of the terrestrial segment covered by all non-natural land uses. See “land use intensity” for more detail.
The two bands must be interpreted together. The intensity value is conditional on the broad land use assigned to the segment, and the intensity of Untransformed lands will be refined separately using ecological pressure and condition information.

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
section: Segment vs. grid broad land cover composition
text:
Segment vs. grid broad land cover composition
We examined land cover composition in a northern Limpopo case study in a mixed use landscape to assess whether segments capture more coherent land use units than a regular 1 × 1 km grid. For each unit, we calculated the proportion of mapped terrestrial area occupied by each broad NLC category and applied the same >20% allocation thresholds and priority rules. Composition was then averaged within each assigned class, giving each unit equal weight.
Segments contained higher mean proportions of their assigned land cover (FIg. 1) than grid cells for settlements, timber plantations, tree croplands and croplands. Both approaches produced predominantly untransformed cover within Protected and Untransformed units. These preliminary results suggest that segments better separate broad land uses in this landscape.



Figure 1. Mean broad land cover composition of segments and 1 × 1 km grid cells by assigned BII land use class in the Limpopo case study. Colours represent underlying land cover; protected status is applied separately during allocation and therefore does not appear as a land-cover category.


The assigned land use class also matched the dominant underlying land cover more frequently in segments than in grid cells, particularly for croplands, tree croplands and settlements. This indicates that segment-based labels more often represent the largest land cover component within an assessment unit. The comparison measures agreement between allocation and mapped composition, rather than classification accuracy.



Figure 2. Percentage of segments and 1 × 1 km grid cells in which the assigned BII land use class matches the dominant underlying land cover in the Limpopo case study. Dominance denotes the largest share of mapped terrestrial area. Protected lands are excluded because protection is an overlapping management designation rather than a land cover category.


We further explored what typically co-occurs with each broad land use class within each segments (Fig. 3).In this case study, untransformed land accounts for approximately 75–100% of the pooled remainder within segments assigned to settlements, croplands, tree croplands and timber plantations. The remainder therefore mainly reflects mixtures of transformed and untransformed cover, although other agricultural uses also contribute, particularly within tree cropland segments. Conversely, the transformed remainder within untransformed-assigned segments consists mainly of croplands and settlements. These percentages describe the remainder rather than the whole segment, and highlight why the condition of untransformed cover may matter when estimating intensity across mixed landscapes.



Figure 3. Broad land cover composition of the pooled area remaining after excluding each segment’s assigned broad class. Panels show assigned classes, with segments grouped by the proportion of terrestrial area occupied by that class (<50%, 50–<80%, and 80–100%). Colours represent each remaining cover’s share of the pooled remainder hectares; segments with no remainder are excluded.
